title: 2-Stage Cooling Process: 135°F to 70°F to 41°F Rules
summary: The 2-stage cooling process: cool food from 135°F to 70°F in 2 hours, then to 41°F within 6 hours total. Where teams slip, and what the 2026 Food Code adds.
body_markdown:
## Executive summary: what to know about two-stage cooling


- The two-stage cooling process in the[FDA Food Code (§ 3-501.14)](https://www.fda.gov/food/fda-food-code/food-code-2026) requires cooked TCS food to cool from 135°F to 70°F within 2 hours, then to 41°F or below within 6 hours total.


- Food that misses 70°F at the 2-hour mark can’t keep cooling. The accepted fix is to reheat it to 165°F and start over, or discard it.
- Food made from room-temperature ingredients, such as tuna salad, follows a one-stage rule: 41°F or below within 4 hours.
- The 2026 Food Code keeps these limits and adds two options: cooling uncovered food at a depth of 2 inches or less, and alternative methods a regulator approves, including refrigeration with continuous electronic monitoring.
- Most misses come from deep pans, early lids, crowded walk-ins and no reading at the 2-hour mark, so the fix for multi-location operators is a logged mid-point check at every store, backed by the free[Safe Temperatures Wall Card](https://sttransactcmsprodcus.blob.core.windows.net/uploads/boha_safe_temperatures_tcs_food_wall_card_83356bc665.pdf) with both cooling stages posted on every prep line.


## What is the two-stage cooling process?


**The two-stage cooling process is the**[FDA Food Code](https://www.fda.gov/food/fda-food-code/food-code-2026) **rule for cooling cooked**[time/temperature control for safety (TCS) food:](https://www.transact-tech.com/resources/blog/what-are-tcs-foods) **cool it from 135°F to 70°F within 2 hours, then to 41°F or below within 6 hours total.** Time saved in the first stage carries over, so food that reaches 70°F in 1 hour has up to 5 more hours to reach 41°F.


Most kitchen teams can recite that rule. Where they slip is the checkpoint in the middle: if nobody takes a reading at the 2-hour mark, a batch that missed 70°F keeps cooling as if nothing happened. This guide covers why the rule splits at 70°F, where real kitchens miss the checkpoint, what the 2026 Food Code changes and how multi-location operators make the check happen every time.


## Why the cooling rule splits at 70°F


The split follows how bacteria grow. Within the[temperature danger zone](https://www.transact-tech.com/resources/blog/temperature-danger-zone) of 41°F to 135°F, growth is fastest between roughly 125°F and 70°F, so the first stage forces food through that band quickly and the second stage finishes the job more gradually. A batch that cools slowly but steadily, taking three hours to reach 70°F, has already failed the rule, even if it reaches 41°F well inside 6 hours.


If food hasn’t reached 70°F at the 2-hour mark, it can’t simply keep cooling. The accepted corrective action is to reheat it to 165°F and start the cooling clock over, or discard it. Food that reaches 70°F on time but is still above 41°F at the 6-hour mark should be discarded. There’s no partial credit for close enough.


### Foods that cool in one stage


Not every TCS food goes through two stages. Food prepared from ingredients at room temperature, such as tuna salad or reconstituted foods, must cool to 41°F or below within 4 hours. The same 4-hour limit applies to TCS food that was legally delivered above 41°F, such as milk or shell eggs received at up to 45°F[(§ 3-501.14)](https://www.fda.gov/food/fda-food-code/food-code-2026) .


## Where cooling breaks down in a real kitchen


The rule itself is simple to state. What consistently trips up real kitchens is a handful of specific, physical mistakes that have nothing to do with understanding the rule and everything to do with how food is actually handled during the cooling process.


**Batch size that's too large for the cooling method.** A deep, tightly packed pan of chili or stew insulates itself. The center of a four-inch-deep pan can take hours longer to reach 70°F than the edges, even though a probe thermometer touched near the surface might suggest it's cooling on schedule. Splitting large batches into smaller, shallower pans is one of the single highest-impact fixes available, and one of the most commonly skipped, because it takes more pan space and more handling.


**Covering food too early.** It's a natural instinct to lid a pan of hot food before putting it in the walk-in, both for cleanliness and to avoid dripping onto other items. But a tight lid traps heat and slows cooling exactly during the highest-risk window. The Food Code allows food to stay[loosely covered or uncovered while it cools](https://www.fda.gov/food/fda-food-code/food-code-2026) , as long as it’s protected from overhead contamination, so cover it once it’s through the first stage.


**Overcrowding the cooler during the cooling window.** A walk-in that's already near capacity struggles to pull heat out of a new pan of hot food efficiently, which slows the whole batch's descent through both stages. Reserving specific cooler space, or using a blast chiller, for actively cooling items, separate from already-cold storage, keeps the highest-risk items cooling at the rate they need to.


**No ice bath or cooling wand for liquid-based items.** Soups, sauces, and stocks cool far faster in an ice bath with occasional stirring than sitting in a cooler on their own. Skipping this step for the sake of time during a busy shift is one of the most common ways a stage-one deadline gets missed.


**No second checkpoint.** Teams that check temperature once, at the start of cooling, and again at the end of service prep the next day, have no way of knowing whether the two-hour, 70°F checkpoint was actually hit. Without a mid-process check, a missed stage-one deadline is invisible until it's already too late to correct.


## What the 2026 Food Code changes for cooling


The 2026 FDA Food Code keeps both cooling limits from the 2022 edition. What changes is the list of approved cooling methods in § 3-501.15, which already includes shallow pans, smaller portions, ice baths, rapid-cooling equipment and adding ice as an ingredient.


- **A new listed method:** cooling uncovered food at a depth of 2 inches or less. FDA added a study to the code’s references finding that[uncovered food cooled at about 2 inches or less poses little risk of pathogen growth](https://www.fda.gov/food/fda-food-code/summary-changes-2026-fda-food-code) .


- **A path for alternative methods:** a new paragraph lets the regulatory authority approve another way to cool cooked TCS food, including refrigeration with[continuous electronic monitoring of time and ambient air temperature.](https://www.food-safety.com/articles/11843-fda-releases-2026-food-code-with-updates-on-food-defense-employee-illness-food-safety-management)


Neither change applies until your state or locality adopts the 2026 edition, and adoption takes years in many places. Stores in different states may follow different editions for a while, so write one cooling procedure that meets the stricter rule and check[where your states stand.](https://www.fda.gov/food/fda-food-code/adoption-fda-food-code-state-and-territorial-agencies-responsible-oversight-restaurants-and-retail)


## How often improper cooling causes outbreaks


Cooling failures aren't a hypothetical risk.[CDC national outbreak data](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/74/ss/ss7401a1.htm) tracking contributing factors to foodborne illness outbreaks from 2014 through 2022 shows improper cooling holding fairly steady as a contributing factor across the first two periods studied, at 9.4% (2014-2016) and 8.8% (2017-2019), before jumping to 10.9% in the most recent period (2020-2022). For bacterial outbreaks specifically, improper cooling wasn't even in the top five contributing factors in the earlier two periods, but climbed to 17.3% in 2020-2022, a significant enough shift that it's worth every multi-location operator's attention, not just a compliance footnote.


The CDC report doesn’t explain the increase, but it coincides with a period of heavy turnover and staffing pressure across foodservice, which are the conditions that make a mid-window checkpoint easy to skip when a kitchen is short-staffed and moving fast.


## Building checkpoints into the two-stage process


The fix isn't retraining staff on the rule itself, since most already know the basic shape of it. What's missing is building physical and procedural checkpoints that catch a miss before it becomes a six-hour failure discovered the next morning.


**A mid-process temperature check, not just a start and end check.** Someone needs to verify the 70°F mark was hit within two hours, logged with an actual time and temperature, not assumed.


**A default maximum batch and pan-depth standard,** so the cooling method itself doesn't quietly work against the timeline before anyone realizes it.


**A clear, posted decision tree for a missed checkpoint:** reheat and restart, or discard, with no ambiguity about which applies and who has the authority to make that call in the moment.


**Cooling logged as its own event,** separate from the hot-holding or storage log it eventually feeds into, so a review can isolate exactly where in the two-stage process a specific batch actually was at each checkpoint.


## Multi-location consistency: same rule, different kitchens


A single kitchen with a strong culture can hold this discipline through habit and hands-on supervision. Across dozens or hundreds of locations, that same discipline needs a system behind it, because the rule doesn't bend for a kitchen that's short-staffed, and an inspector reviewing site 40 isn't going to accept "we usually do it right" as documentation.

## Where this fits into a broader temperature program


Cooling is one piece of a larger temperature program that covers receiving, storage, cold holding, hot holding and reheating, all built around the same[temperature danger zone](https://www.transact-tech.com/resources/blog/temperature-danger-zone) of 41°F to 135°F. ## Frequently asked questions


### What is the two-stage cooling rule under the FDA Food Code?


Cooked TCS food must cool from 135°F to 70°F within 2 hours (stage one), then to 41°F or below within 6 hours total from 135°F (stage two). Any time saved in stage one carries over to stage two.


### What happens if food doesn't reach 70°F within two hours?


It can’t continue cooling past the missed checkpoint. The accepted corrective action is to reheat it to 165°F and restart the cooling process, or discard it.


### Why does pan depth matter for cooling food safely?


Deeper, more tightly packed pans insulate the food at the center, slowing heat loss significantly compared to shallow pans. A deep pan can miss the two-hour, 70°F checkpoint even when a surface-level temperature reading looks fine, because the center is cooling much more slowly.


### How common is improper cooling as a cause of foodborne illness outbreaks?


CDC national outbreak data shows improper cooling was a contributing factor in roughly 9% to 11% of tracked outbreaks between 2014 and 2022, and climbed to 17.3% of bacterial outbreaks specifically in the most recent period studied (2020-2022), a notable increase worth attention from any multi-location operator.


### What's the fastest way to cool a large batch of soup or sauce safely?


An ice bath with occasional stirring, combined with splitting the batch into smaller containers, is typically the fastest and most reliable method for liquid-based items, significantly outperforming simply placing a covered pot in a walk-in cooler.


### If food cools to 70°F in 1 hour, how long does it have to reach 41°F?


Up to 5 more hours. The Food Code sets a total of 6 hours from 135°F to 41°F, so time saved in the first stage carries over to the second.


### A batch of chili cooled from 135°F to 82°F in two hours. What should be done?


It missed the 70°F checkpoint, so it can’t keep cooling. Reheat it to 165°F and start the cooling process over, or discard it.


### Can food be left uncovered while it cools?


Yes. The Food Code allows food to be loosely covered or uncovered during cooling if it’s protected from overhead contamination. Covering it tightly too early traps heat and slows cooling.


### How long can food made from room-temperature ingredients take to cool?


4 hours. TCS food prepared from ingredients at room temperature, such as tuna salad, must reach 41°F or below within 4 hours.


### What changed for cooling in the 2026 FDA Food Code?


The time and temperature limits didn’t change. The 2026 edition adds cooling uncovered food at a depth of 2 inches or less as a listed method and lets regulators approve alternative cooling methods, including refrigeration with continuous electronic monitoring.
